detail_rows: Minimum :: 4.0 ft NAVD88, for any new or replaced seawall or dock, publicly or privately owned. | Maximum :: 6.0 ft NAVD88. | Build for more :: Standard 3 requires the wall to be designed and constructed so a further 12 to 18 inches can be added later and the wall stays structurally sound without altering it. | Watch the datum :: The city states its requirement in NAVD88. title: Seawall Permits in Boca Raton

qualifier: Boca inspects in a set order and one of them happens before the cap goes on. Miss it and the cap comes off, so the sequence matters more here than the paperwork does.
detail_rows: Inspection one, before the cap :: A zoning location survey showing the seawall wetface or bulkhead line, the property line and the pile locations. It must be approved before the structural cap and piling inspections can even be scheduled. | Inspection two, after construction :: A final engineer report giving the seawall cap elevation, confirming the work matches the permit drawings, with photographs of the finished wall. | If there is a dock or lift too :: A separate final marine structure survey, plus the location survey before framing. All three inspections apply when the job covers both. | What the plans must show :: The existing wetface or bulkhead line, the property line, the distance from the cap edge and from any marine structure to both, existing and proposed panels and piles, and the finished elevation of the top of the cap. | Where the rules live :: Chapter 22 of the Code of Ordinances for marine structures, and Engineering Design Standards Manual section 7.7 for the elevations. | Budget for a bond :: Some cities in South Florida require a refundable bond on top of the contract price. Ask Boca early whether yours needs one, because it sits on top of the contract price.
source: City of Boca Raton, Seawalls and Marine Structures permitting guidance (Development Services, Zoning); Engineering Design Standards Manual § 7.7; Code of Ordinances Ch. 22

title: Seawall Permits in Delray Beach

qualifier: A permit is required to build a new seawall or alter an existing one. Delray asks for three things before it will issue one, and the third is the one that catches people out — the outside agencies have to sign off first, and chasing them is your job, not the city's.
detail_rows: What the city needs :: A survey showing the seawall's location and elevation in relation to the adjoining land, water and channels. | Who draws the plans :: A professional engineer registered in Florida. The plans must be sealed. | The step people miss :: Approval from the applicable reviewing agencies before the building permit is issued. The code puts that on the applicant, not the city. | When the whole wall gets pulled in :: If the work counts as substantial repair, the minimum elevation applies to the continuous seawall along the entire shoreline, not just the stretch you are fixing. | Substantial repair, definition one :: Work on more than 50% of the length of the structure, seawall and cap included. | Substantial repair, definition two :: Any work that changes the elevation along more than 50% of the length. | Keeping it in repair :: A seawall is presumed to be in disrepair if it lets upland soil erode, lets material pass through, or lets tidal water run unimpeded onto neighbouring property. That falls under Chapter 100, Nuisances, Section 100.04.
source: City of Delray Beach Land Development Regulations Sec. 7.1.7(D) and (E); Ordinance 23-21, adopted 11 January 2022

qualifier: A seawall and a dock priced together are a different job from either one alone, and the number moves on things you can establish before anyone quotes. We do not publish a figure, because a price given without a survey of what is standing is a guess wearing a dollar sign. What we can tell you is exactly what moves it.
detail_rows: Condition of what is standing :: Whether the existing wall can be repaired or has to be replaced is the single biggest fork in the price. A survey answers it; a phone call cannot. | Demolition and removal :: Taking out an old dock and its timber piles is its own line. Piles pulled, not cut, cost more and are usually the right answer. | Access :: Whether a barge can reach the shoreline, or the work has to come through the property, changes mobilisation before a single panel is set. | Elevation target :: Building to 4 ft NAVD88 now versus straight to 5 ft changes steel and concrete today, and decides whether the wall comes up again before 2050. | Decking selection :: Composite varies widely by product. Ask for the per-square-foot rate and the exact product name in the bid. | Return walls :: Often not known until the wall is exposed. Ask for it priced as a conditional line rather than discovered later. | What to ask for :: A bid broken into demolition, wall, cap, dock and decking as separate lines. Two bids far apart almost always differ in one of them.
